articles.title: In 2022, a hydrologist’s team launched 40 floating wetlands made from bamboo, foam and discarded materials across Nepal’s polluted Nagdaha Lake; after five months, native flowering plants cut nitrate by up to 94% and iron by 95%
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Discover how innovative floating wetlands made from bamboo and recycled materials are dramatically improving water quality in Nagdaha Lake, Nepal, reducing nitrate and iron levels by up to 94% and 95%, respectively.
articles.body: Nagdaha Lake, a small body of water in the Kathmandu Valley in the Lalitpur district, was once used by the locals for daily tasks, irrigation, and washing. Like many urban lakes in South Asia, it has been absorbing runoff from the nearby settlements for the past few decades, absorbing household waste, agricultural fertiliser, and seepage from grazing land until nutrient levels reached a point where the lake was choked with algae and deprived of oxygen. Over the years, local advocacy groups attempted several cleanup initiatives, but because the underlying nutrient load in the water was never truly eliminated, eutrophication kept coming back.A new form of intervention came at the end of 2022, when a hydrologist and her team of researchers set out to see if the lake could effectively be given its own artificial root system. Dr. Soni M. Pradhanang, a hydrologist at the University of Rhode Island, was one of the collaborators on the project, which was led by Professor Sadhana Pradhanang. The design of 40 floating platforms made from bamboo frames, foam layers and matting, using recycled or locally sourced materials where possible.Transforming waste materials into a functional filterFloating treatment wetland is a horticultural concept rather than an engineering one; however, the chemistry beneath is quite advanced. The underside of the raft is covered by a dense, tangled surface of hanging roots, which provides a perfect habitat for biofilm, a thin layer of bacteria that thrives in the root zone. Together, the roots of the plants and the bacteria that live there pull dissolved nutrients straight from the surrounding water, pulling out chemicals such as nitrate and phosphate that would otherwise feed algal blooms.Because the rafts float on the water surface, their submerged root networks remain in direct contact with the water column rather than sitting on the lakebed.The project, funded through the Asia Pacific Network for Global Change Research, deliberately used discarded and low-cost materials to keep the approach replicable in communities with limited environmental budgets. The rafts were built and installed by local youth groups and volunteers along with the study team. For buoyancy they used styrofoam rescued from packaging, and for the structural frame they used bamboo. The project also involved local youth groups and volunteers in preparing and installing the rafts, since their visible presence gave residents and local government officials a tangible way to observe and understand a pollution remediation technology that might otherwise have remained an abstract research exercise.What the monitoring data showed after months in the waterThe team's researchers regularly monitored the water around the rafts to see how nutrient and metal concentrations changed over time, and the results after a few months of operation were stunning. Field monitoring revealed nitrate reductions up to ninety-four percent and a reduction of about ninety-five percent in dissolved iron levels in the treated parts of the lake. A separate 2025 study of polluted Hanumante River water in Nepal found nitrate removal rates of about 86% to 88% in floating treatment wetlands using several plant species, with some systems also removing more than 60% of iron.Not everything with the project went so easily, and that in itself is a helpful reminder that ecological engineering is not a linear process. The team had to replant hundreds of specimens after one of the two plant species withered during a seasonal transition and again the following year to keep the system operating. The project also produced a practical model that other sites can adapt.The regional FTWS project also involved collaborators in Bangladesh and India, and its guidebook provides practical guidance for adapting the technology to different sites and countries.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.summary: News News: Indian troops along with soldiers from 20 other nations are taking part in one of Indo-Pacific's largest multinational military exercises in terms of .
articles.body: Indian troops along with soldiers from 20 other nations are taking part in one of Indo-Pacific's largest multinational military exercises in terms of countries involved The wargames called Exercise Super Garuda Shield 2026, is nearing its end in the Indonesian archipelago, according to local media. Running from August 31 to September 11, the annual exercise has brought together 4,743 personnel who working through 12 separate training modules at multiple sites across the island chain.India's contribution has come in the form of 40 paratroopers as per reports from Indonesia. The report also mentions that Indian soldiers along with American, New Zealand and Indonesian troops participated in a joint "Special Operation Forces (SOF) Flat Range Advance Shooting" drill at the Indonesian Army's Combat Training Center in Martapura, South Sumatra. In all, 270 personnel took part in this active firing event along with 110 Indonesian troops, 80 American troops, 45 from New Zealand and 40 Indian soldiers, running through advanced live-fire drills designed to sharpen marksmanship, combat effectiveness and coordination in joint operational scenarios. The exercise wrapped up without incident.Beyond the shooting range, Indian troops also featured in the exercise's airborne segment. Indian paratroopers joined their Indonesian, American, Japanese and French counterparts in a static-line parachute exercise in which jumps were conducted from low altitudes of 1,200 feet over the Baturaja landing area in South Sumatra, one of several joint training activities designed to test how well partner militaries can operate together on short notice, as per Jakarta.Indonesian Armed Forces Commander General Agus Subiyanto said the broader exercise is meant to test operational readiness, deepen defence diplomacy and sharpen partner militaries' ability to respond to emerging security challenges, a description that captures just how far Super Garuda Shield has grown beyond a routine bilateral drill. Besides India, Indonesia and the US, participating nations this year include Australia, Japan, France, UK, Canada, South Korea, Singapore, Thailand and several other regional and partner countries, as per Indonesian media.For India, the exercise fits into a much bigger picture of strengthening ties with Indonesia under the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership. Jakarta has recently procured India's BrahMos supersonic cruise missile and become the first export customer for the Astra air-to-air missile, both signs of how far the defence relationship between the two countries has come. New Delhi and Jakarta also increasingly see eye to eye on maritime security and freedom of navigation across the Indo-Pacific, particularly around the strategically vital Malacca Strait. Multinational exercises like Super Garuda Shield continue to give India and its regional partners a working platform to build on that cooperation, one live-fire drill and parachute jump at a time.

articles.title: In 2023, Seville adapted a 3,000-year-old underground water technique to cool a renovated amphitheatre; the system uses solar power, water and underground cooling
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In a bold move against soaring temperatures, Seville has innovatively revived the ancient qanat system, cooling air in an abandoned amphitheatre with a temperature drop from 104°F to 63°F using solar-powered technology.
articles.body: Seville regularly experiences extreme summer heat, with temperatures frequently approaching 40 degrees Celsius. The Andalusian capital frequently experiences temperatures close to 40 degrees Celsius, or roughly 104 degrees Fahrenheit. Officials there have formally begun naming and categorising heatwaves, just as meteorologists do with hurricanes. A group of engineers and researchers in Seville concluded that a method created thousands of years ago might help address a pressing issue in a climate that scientists predict will only become harsher.That method is the qanat, a network of subterranean tunnels that Persian farmers invented some 3,000 years ago to transport water through parched regions without losing it to evaporation. A project called CartujaQanat has adapted this ancient engineering for a public square and a renovated amphitheatre on a former Expo site on the Isla de la Cartuja. It uses solar power, buried pipes, and the earth's naturally stable temperature to draw cool air up from below ground while the surface bakes overhead.How Seville adapted an ancient irrigation method for coolingThe original Persian qanats relied on gravity and the depth of the tunnels. Persian engineers finally recognised that vertical shafts connected to these tunnels could carry both water and cooled air to the surface. Water went through tunnels that were excavated far enough below the surface to keep soil temperatures cool throughout the year. CartujaQanat reconstructs the same fundamental idea with contemporary materials and a closed water circuit. Water flows through rooftop solar panels and an outdoor aqueduct at night before cooling in underground tanks with stable ground temperatures and cooler night air. During the day, solar-powered pumps force the same water through pipes placed in front of fans, creating an air current that is released into the amphitheatre and plaza through tiny holes in the steps and floor. Engineers working on the project said that the system can lower ground and ambient temperatures at the site by as much as 10 degrees Celsius. The system uses the thermal stability of underground soil and water to cool air before releasing it into the occupied space.Why depth and darkness matter more than machineryUnlike a conventional air conditioner, the system relies on underground thermal storage, water circulation and solar-powered equipment rather than refrigerants and compressors. The site itself sits two metres underground, with a white ceiling that reflects heat and columns and vegetation around it to help keep the temperature down even when the active pumping system is not functioning. Related research on earth-air-water heat-exchanger systems has found that nighttime cooling can lower soil temperatures and help maintain cooler conditions into the next day. That is precisely why the project’s directors say it is fundamentally different from a domestic air conditioner: the entire process depends on solar electricity and the physical properties of soil and water, not refrigerants or compressors. The initiative required substantial investment and combined European urban-innovation funding with support from local institutions. The project combined European urban-innovation funding with support from local institutions.Other hot cities are now watching the project carefully as a modelSeville’s experiment addresses a combination of extreme heat and dense urban development that affects cities across the Mediterranean and other hot regions. Recently, Indian cities have increasingly named and recorded heatwaves, matching the institutional seriousness that Seville initially devoted to the problem. The CartujaQanat project demonstrates that some of the oldest engineering solutions humans developed for arid climates, refined with modern solar power and monitoring rather than replaced by them, may still have a meaningful role to play as summers grow hotter and city budgets for climate adaptation remain limited. The CartujaQanat project shows how underground water infrastructure, solar energy and thermal storage can be combined in a public space to reduce heat exposure without relying entirely on conventional air conditioning.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: AI, quantum navigation & drone swarms: China’s J-50 aims to ‘leapfrog’ fighter technology
articles.summary: International News: China’s next-generation stealth fighters are being designed with advanced autonomous capabilities that could allow them to fly without a pilot, naviga.
articles.body: China’s next-generation stealth fighters are being designed with advanced autonomous capabilities that could allow them to fly without a pilot, navigate without satellite signals and control large groups of drones, according to new research by Chinese military aircraft designers.The research comes from the Shenyang Aircraft Design & Research Institute, linked to the development of the aircraft widely known as the J-50.A paper led by the institute’s chief flight-control designer, Zhang Dong, describes a “leapfrog transformation” in next-generation fighter technology, aimed at moving rapidly to more advanced capabilities instead of developing them step by step.It describes concepts including automatic control if a pilot is incapacitated, quantum navigation when satellite signals are unavailable, and fighter aircraft working with drones for attack, reconnaissance and protection missions.What does the “leapfrog” technology mean?The research points to a major shift in how China wants its next-generation fighters to operate. Instead of relying entirely on a pilot to control the aircraft, the designers are exploring systems that could allow the fighter to take over some tasks automatically and continue operating in difficult combat situations.One example is autonomous flight. If a pilot becomes unconscious or faces an extremely heavy workload, the aircraft could automatically take over control and continue flying. This could help keep the fighter operational even when the pilot is unable to control it normally.The researchers are also looking at navigation without satellite signals. The paper discusses quantum navigation, which could help an aircraft determine its position when systems such as GPS are unavailable or have been disrupted. This is important in a conflict because an enemy could attempt to jam or disable satellite-based navigation.Another major part of the concept is drone teaming. A manned fighter could work with a large number of drones, with the drones taking on different roles such as attack, reconnaissance and protection. Their formation could also be reorganised depending on the changing battlefield situation.China sixth generation fighter programmesChina is developing two major sixth-generation stealth-fighter programmes, represented by aircraft widely known as the J-36 and J-50. Both are still developmental aircraft, and Beijing has not officially confirmed these designations.The two prototypes first attracted global attention after appearing in flight tests in late 2024 and have since undergone further testing.The aircraft widely referred to as the J-36 is being developed by Chengdu Aircraft Corporation. Public images and analysis by defence experts indicate that it has a large, tailless design with three engines. Its size and configuration suggest a focus on long range, stealth and a large weapons payload, although its exact operational role has not been officially disclosed.The aircraft commonly called the J-50 is associated with the Shenyang Aircraft Design & Research Institute and is smaller than the J-36. It has a tailless, twin-engine design and has also undergone flight testing. Images of a later version showed the removal of the nose-mounted air-data boom used during earlier test flights, which analysts viewed as a possible sign of progress in the programme.The two sixth generation aircraft of China reflects two different approaches to sixth-generation airpower. The larger J-36 appears focused on range, payload and stealth, while the smaller J-50 could offer a different combination of agility, flexibility and potentially carrier operations. The parallel programmes also allow China to test different aerodynamic and technological solutions rather than committing to a single design from the beginning.

articles.title: BSP's family drama: Why no 'Anand' for Mayawati ahead of Uttar Pradesh elections?
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Three promotions. Three demotions.  And now staring at a possible exit!Well, that’s how the political scorecard reads for Akash Anand, whos.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Three promotions. Three demotions. And now staring at a possible exit!Well, that’s how the political scorecard reads for Akash Anand, whose “maturity meter” has not just failed him again, but has also put him on the brink of exit from the Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP).7 days after his third demotion, Akash Anand finds himself in a difficult spot, with BSP chief Mayawati opening the doors for his exit from the party. "The people in the party feel that just as he was relieved of all the important responsibilities of the post of national coordinator on September 3, 2026, he should now also be completely freed from the party from today. Therefore, if Akash Anand wants to remain independent in the party, he is free to do so; that is, he has now been completely freed from the party," Mayawati posted on X.This despite the fact that Akash Anand's father-in-law, former Rajya Sabha MP Ashok Siddharth on Thursday bowed before Mayawati's ultimatum and announced his retirement from politics and social life, after the BSP chief linked his "sanyas" to any future reinstatement of responsibilities to her nephew Akash Anand.In an emotional post on X, Siddharth said he was retiring from political and social life "right now", adding that if he ever had to give his life for Mayawati, it would be a matter of pride for him.FIL bends but Mayawati refuses to budgeBut neither Siddharth's actions nor his words made any impact on Mayawati.She questioned Siddharth's intentions, saying his "announcement should have come immediately after her call for him to retire." Mayawati alleged that the delay showed that Siddharth's ambitions and intentions had not changed completely."If Ashok Siddharth had even a little genuine concern for the bright future of his son-in-law Akash Anand and the larger interests of the BSP and its Ambedkarite Bahujan movement, he would have announced his retirement without delay," she said.Mayawati also slammed Anand for not reposting her earlier X post linking his future responsibilities in the party to his father-in-law's retirement. She said Anand had earlier reposted posts from her social media account "to demonstrate his loyalty," but had not done so in this case despite the post being in his own interest.Mayawati said this indicated that both Siddharth and Anand were more attached to personal and family interests than to the success of the party and its movement.She questioned whether Anand could effectively serve the BSP while remaining caught between his family ties and the interests of the party."If Akash Anand is less concerned about the real interests of the party and the movement and his own political career, and more attached to family relationships, then it is natural to ask how he can work for the good of the BSP and the movement while remaining double-minded," she said.Third time unlucky?Akash Anand’s latest demotion was on September 3, when aunt Mayawati announced that her nephew had again lost his political maturity."I have allowed Akash Anand to work in the party, which is before all of you, but Akash Anand still needs to become more mature. Till then, it would not be appropriate to give him a major responsibility in the party," Mayawati said at a national-level meeting of BSP office-bearers.And that ensured Akash Anand, the chief national coordinator of BSP, was back to square one. His Twitter bio reflected the sudden change in his status within the party. From BSP "National Convenor", he became "Party Worker, BSP." Just a few days later, he made yet another edit to his bio, which read: "Party Supporter, BSP." This is how his X bio reads now.It was less than a month back, August 10 to be exact, that Akash Anand had formally launched the BSP’s election campaign for the 2027 Uttar Pradesh assembly elections from Sadabad assembly constituency in Hathras. He addressed a well-attended rally and launched a broadside against the BJP government in Uttar Pradesh over jobs, education and law and order, while taking digs at Congress leader Rahul Gandhi and Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav, calling them both “uncle.”From being anointed Mayawati’s successor to being a party worker and now a party supporter - it has been a tumultuous and bumpy ride for the young Akash Anand. And this time around there is a twist in the tale: Akash’s younger brother Ishan Anand has been brought to the centre stage.(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(message,function(e){if(e.data[datawrapper-height]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(iframe);for(var n in e.data[datawrapper-height])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[datawrapper-height][n]+px;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();On September 3, when Mayawati entered the venue of the meeting of office-bearers, walking behind her was not Akash but his younger brother Ishan. Wearing the BSP's blue sash around his neck, he stood behind his aunt till she settled down.Akash Anand entered politics in 2017 at the young age of 22. Anand, who did his MBA from London, made his political debut with Mayawati at a rally in Uttar Pradesh's Saharanpur, where he shared the dais with Akhilesh Yadav and Ajit Singh.In April 2019, Akash Anand addressed his first rally in Uttar Pradesh's Agra. The BSP was then part of the opposition Mahagathbandhan, an anti-Congress and anti-BJP bloc formed in the run-up to the 2019 general election under the leadership of Akhilesh Yadav and Mayawati with Ajit Singh's Rashtriya Lok Dal.Mayawati appointed him BSP’s national coordinator in June 2019. Since then, it has been a bumpy ride for him. Every promotion since then has been followed by a demotion.Anand's FIL connection and maturity questionAfter 6 days of suspense, Mayawati finally revealed what triggered her against Akash Anand yet again. In a long post on X, Mayawati explained how Akash Anand had once again, after two years, lost his “political maturity.” And also, what he could do to get it back.The trigger this time around was Ashok Siddharth, the father in law of Akash Anand. Ashok Siddharth was expelled by Maywati from BSP last month for the second time over indiscipline and anti-party stance.Taking to X, the BSP supremo wrote: “It is well known that Ashok Siddharth had previously been expelled for indiscipline and violating guidelines, specifically regarding the distribution of party tickets and a failure to coordinate properly with BSP Maharashtra state president during state elections. He had been reinstated on the condition that he would not repeat such mistakes and would be assigned responsibility of expanding the party's support base only in other states, not in Uttar Pradesh.”She also informed that Ashok Siddharth will not be taken back into the party “under any circumstances in the future”.Hardening her stand further against Ashok Siddharth, Mayawati stated that a clear path remains for Akash Anand to resume an active leadership role within the movement, provided Siddharth steps aside completely."In such a situation, keeping in mind the interests of the BSP Party and Movement, as well as his own family and the future of his son-in-law Shri Akash Anand, Shri Ashok Siddharth still has the opportunity to renounce his political ambitions, rise above personal interests, etc., and completely retire from politics. Only then will Shri Akash Anand be able to work freely in the party, and only then will the party sympathetically consider restoring his responsibilities so that he can play an active role in the party—this is the general consensus in the party," Mayawati said in her post.Urging people from the Dalit community, to not engage in any action driven by personal or familial interests that creates obstacles in their path, for which “history may not forgive them," Mayawati cited Ashok Siddharth as a prime example of an official prioritising "personal and familial interests and ambitions over the BSP's mission, despite receiving multiple opportunities to reform."The party gave him not just one but several opportunities to mend his ways, but he prioritised his personal and familial interests and ambitions over the BSP's mission, the consequences of which he himself, along with his son-in-law Shri Akash Anand, has had to bear," Mayawati said in her statement.Can BSP afford this 'family drama'?With the UP assembly elections just months away, a family drama is the last thing that the BSP cadres in the state would have hoped for. The party’s trajectory in the state has been downhill. In the 2022 assembly elections, the BSP could win just 1 seat with a vote share of 12.88%. This was a sharp decline from the 19 seats and a 22.23% vote share that Mayawati had got in 2017.(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(message,function(e){if(e.data[datawrapper-height]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(iframe);for(var n in e.data[datawrapper-height])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[datawrapper-height][n]+px;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();The 2024 Lok Sabha elections went on to showcase that Mayawati’s dismal 2022 performance was not an aberration. The BSP supporters have dwindled and some have even changed loyalties, but what remains still strong is Mayawati’s appeal and popularity among the party’s cadres.However, the 2027 challenge is going to be tough for Maywati and her BSP. articles.title: West Virginia's restored elk herd is finally roaming farther; here's how a conservation comeback is changing the landscape
articles.summary: US News: Nearly a decade after elk were returned to West Virginia, the growing herd is beginning to venture beyond its familiar range, offering a new sign of h.
articles.body: Nearly a decade after elk were returned to West Virginia, the growing herd is beginning to venture beyond its familiar range, offering a new sign of how far the state’s ambitious wildlife restoration effort has come. The movement was highlighted by WV MetroNews, which reported in July that wildlife officials are seeing more elk explore beyond the Tomblin Wildlife Management Area in Logan County. The West Virginia Division of Natural Resources (WVDNR), meanwhile, says the restoration programme has brought the herd to about 130 animals and recorded at least 60 native calf births since the project began. One young female recently travelled north into Lincoln County near Harts Creek, spending time along a ridge and in a pasture on private farmland before returning to the Tomblin area. Wildlife officials were able to follow her movements through GPS telemetry. The journey is significant not because elk are suddenly spreading across the state, but because it shows individual animals are beginning to test the wider landscape available to them.From disappearing species to a growing herdElk once roamed widely across West Virginia but disappeared from the state by the late 1800s, largely because of overhunting and habitat loss. The modern restoration effort began after years of studies identified the southern coalfields as particularly suitable for elk. Large areas affected by surface mining had created open habitat, while relatively limited agricultural land reduced the likelihood of conflicts with farmers.In December 2016, the WVDNR released its first 24 elk at Tomblin Wildlife Management Area, marking the animals’ return after more than 140 years. The state subsequently added another 95 elk, 53 from Kentucky and 42 from Arizona, beginning in 2018. Additional releases in 2024 brought the estimated herd to about 130 animals. Since the programme began, at least 60 calves have been born in West Virginia.Why are the elk starting to wander?For now, Tomblin remains the centre of the herd’s range. But as the population grows, some animals are beginning to look for their own territory. GPS collars fitted to released elk, along with collars placed on previously unmarked animals, allow biologists to follow where they travel and how they use the landscape.The recent movements into Lincoln County therefore give researchers a glimpse of what the next phase of the restoration could look like. West Virginia’s designated Elk Management Area already covers about 2,845 square miles, spanning all of Logan, Mingo, McDowell and Wyoming counties and parts of Boone, Lincoln and Wayne counties.The state’s management strategy calls for officials to monitor elk movements around those boundaries and consider adjustments if the animals’ use of the wider landscape changes significantly.A conservation comeback that is also drawing visitorsThe return of elk has transformed the animals into both a conservation success and a growing tourism attraction. The WVDNR’s 2026 Elk Management Tours are scheduled to begin on September 13, with guided four-hour excursions continuing on weekends through October 24. The tours take visitors into elk country around Logan County, where park staff explain the animals’ behaviour, history and conservation.A viewing platform and education centre at Tomblin Wildlife Management Area, opened in 2025, have added another way for visitors to see the herd while learning about the restoration effort.The broader significance of the programme, however, lies beyond tourism. A species that vanished from West Virginia more than a century ago is now reproducing in the wild, establishing a home range and beginning to explore beyond it. For conservationists, those wandering elk may be among the clearest signs yet that the restoration is no longer simply about bringing the animals back, it is about watching them become part of the landscape again.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Zelensky says Ukraine has struck new targets in Russia
articles.summary: Ukraine has once again attacked several infrastructure targets in Russia, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Thursday. Eight infrastructure objec...
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Zelensky announced that Ukraine has targeted eight infrastructure objects in Russia, including an oil refinery and a commercial port, in response to the ongoing conflict between the two countries.

A woman was killed in a Ukrainian drone strike in the Voronezh region, with two others injured, while falling drone debris from attacks in Dagestan and the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous District caused fires at port infrastructure and a theatre.

Ukraine has been using drones to counterattack against Russia, which has been engaged in a war with Ukraine for over four and a half years, with recent strikes targeting various regions in Russia.

Ukraine has once again attacked several infrastructure targets in Russia, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Thursday.

Eight infrastructure objects serving the Russian war effort were targeted, Zelensky wrote on social media.

He said an oil refinery in the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous District and a commercial port in the Russian Republic of Dagestan were hit. Facilities in the Moscow, Voronezh, Astrakhan and Bryansk regions were also targeted, Zelensky wrote, without providing details.

In the Voronezh region, a woman was killed in a Ukrainian drone strike in the city of Borisoglebsk, according to Governor Alexsandr Gusev. Two further people were injured, he said, adding that 19 Ukrainian drones had been intercepted over the region.

Dagestan's acting head of republic, Fyodor Shchukin, said that falling drone debris had started fires at port infrastructure and at a theatre in Makhachkala. There were no casualties, he said.

There were reports the previous day of a drone strike in the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous District in western Siberia, far from Ukraine. District Governor Dmitry Artyukhov said that falling drone debris had caused a fire at an unspecified industrial facility.

Russia has been waging a devastating war against Ukraine for more than four and a half years. As part of its defence effort, Ukraine has stepped up its counterattacks in recent months, primarily using drones.

articles.title: A Newport mansion is being restored with a staircase technique dating to the 1500s; instead of modern exposed fasteners, craftsmen lock the wooden steps together with mortises and wedges
articles.summary: US News: A stairway goes up to nowhere in a woodshop. No grand foyer at the bottom, no upper floor waiting at the top—just a full-scale helical structure surro.
articles.body: A stairway goes up to nowhere in a woodshop. No grand foyer at the bottom, no upper floor waiting at the top—just a full-scale helical structure surrounded by tools, machinery, and carefully prepared pieces of wood. But this unfinished staircase is also something much more: an intersection of centuries-old craftsmanship and contemporary engineering. Wondering what it is? Well, there is a stairway being built for the restoration of a historic home in Newport, Rhode Island. It is a Mark Richey Woodworking’s design and a revival of a late 16th century European method of building stairs, and uses modern computer modeling and manufacturing technology to achieve accurate results. According to an online report by Markrichey website, Newport is known for its grand Gilded Age homes, famously and somewhat facetiously referred to as “summer cottages.” Buildings like The Breakers, Miramar and Hammersmith Farm helped make the city a showcase of American architectural history. And this private residence being restored has undergone many renovations over the years. The current owners wanted to modernize the property but keep the character and craftsmanship that was part of the original design, states the online report.This went beyond just copying an old-fashioned look, as the architectural team also wanted construction techniques that would allow for the durability, precision and visual cleanliness of historic restoration. And that is when Mark Richey Woodworking was brought onto the project for its architectural millwork expertise and its knowledge of traditional woodworking methods.A 16th-century technique finds a modern revivalThe project’s heart is a dramatic helical staircase with laminated curved stringers and mortised-and-wedged treads and risers. As per reports, the technique originated in the construction of European staircases in the late 1500s, when wealthy homes and castles had elaborate staircases. This method does not use visible screws or nails to hold the finished treads and risers like many modern site-built stairs. Instead, each tread fits into a precisely cut recess—a mortise—and wooden wedges, glued in place on either side in the stringers, hold the components together. The result is a self-securing structure, each tread/riser assembly provides stability for the next. A hidden connection can also be used from below at the tongue and groove joint, but the finished walking surfaces are free of exposed fasteners.Made to move with the buildingHistoric buildings with wood framing are especially problematic, as they are never truly static. Wood expands and contracts with the seasons. Buildings settle, framing can shift over time. Face-fastened treads on notched stringers are common in conventional stairs and can cause gaps, squeaks and the look of filled screw or nail holes as these movements occur. The installation can be more difficult because the individual pieces often require a lot of fitting on the construction site. Another way to go is mortised-and-wedged construction. The technique aims to keep the joints tight by mechanically locking the wooden components together and to produce a strong, rigid assembly that can span considerable distances without additional support. The method offers both structural and esthetic benefits for a historic residence where appearance and longevity are equally important.Old craftsmanship comes back with technologyThe staircase is built in an old way of construction, but its creation is based on modern technology. Mark Richey Woodworking works with architects and builders during the design phase, helping to translate lofty architectural visions into components that can be manufactured. Engineers model complex shapes on 3D CAD systems and can check the design before starting fabrication. As per the online report, computer-controlled machinery produces components with the accuracy required for complex joinery, while skilled craftsmen do the fitting, laminating and finishing. This mix also reduces uncertainty at time of installation. The workshop can provide the staircase as a carefully engineered kit of parts, rather than shipping out unfinished components for extensive adjustment on the construction site.A full-scale rehearsal workshopFor especially complicated projects, the team is able to bring the actual environment of the staircase into the workshop. Full height temporary walls are constructed to the same radius and footprint as the actual stairwell. The complete helical stair for the Newport residence was preassembled in the shop and trucked to the property. This enabled the craftsmen to identify potential problems and check that the components fitted together before installation. And the result is a brilliant example of how historic craftsmanship does not necessarily mean something from the past. Mortises and wedges, a time-honored woodworking method, can be adapted to modern construction through CAD modeling, CNC machinery and precise hand-fitting, maintaining the character of a historic American home.Images Courtesy: MarkricheyCatch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Tax startup CEO allegedly faked CPA credentials and company revenue to raise $13.3 million; investors lost everything as funds paid for a home, Tesla and Caribbean wedding
articles.summary: US News: Federal agents arrested the former head of a Los Angeles tax compliance startup in Fort Lauderdale, Florida, as she was trying to board a luxury cruis.
articles.body: Federal agents arrested the former head of a Los Angeles tax compliance startup in Fort Lauderdale, Florida, as she was trying to board a luxury cruise ship. She has been charged with defrauding venture capital funds of more than $13 million (£10 million). Shiloh Luckey, 42, also known as Shiloh Johnson, was arrested on Sunday and later released on bond by a federal court in Florida, according to a press release from the United States Attorney’s Office for the Central District of California. Federal prosecutors allege that Luckey tricked investors into putting money into her now-defunct company, ComplYant App Inc, by falsely claiming she was a licensed certified public accountant (CPA) and making up the company’s recurring revenue figures. Prosecutors say that instead of building a genuine technology business, Luckey used investor money to fund an expensive lifestyle, including an Inglewood property, a Tesla and a luxury wedding on the Caribbean island of Anguilla.Arrest at the cruise terminalAccording to details released by the US Department of Justice, a federal grand jury in Los Angeles returned a 15-count indictment against Luckey on September 1. The charges include nine counts of securities fraud, three counts of wire fraud, one count of bank fraud and two counts of money laundering. The Federal Bureau of Investigation, which is leading the investigation, arrested Luckey in Florida before she could leave on vacation. She is expected to appear before a judge at the United States District Court in downtown Los Angeles in the coming weeks. If convicted on all charges, Luckey faces up to 30 years in federal prison for bank fraud, up to 20 years for each count of securities and wire fraud, and up to 10 years for each count of money laundering.Phantom clients and fake credentialsCourt documents describe what prosecutors say was a planned, multi-year fraud carried out in the Los Angeles technology sector. Luckey founded ComplYant in 2019 and marketed the app as a digital tool that helped small businesses manage complex tax requirements through a monthly subscription model. Between September 2020 and September 2023, Luckey pitched the software to venture capital investors. Prosecutors allege that she used false pitch decks, made-up financial updates and inflated cash balances to make ComplYant appear to be a fast-growing and highly profitable software company. To build trust with investors, Luckey repeatedly claimed that she was a licensed CPA with extensive experience in corporate accounting and tax strategy. However, federal prosecutors said in the indictment that Luckey had never been licensed as a CPA. Investors were allegedly misled by the false financial figures and claims about her qualifications. Venture capital groups eventually invested more than $13.3 million in the company.A house of cards built on bad checksFederal authorities also allege that Luckey carried out a check-kiting scheme in late 2022 to buy her home in Inglewood, California. During September and October 2022, Luckey allegedly wrote a $1.5 million check from a ComplYant bank account that did not have enough money to cover it. She deposited the check into another ComplYant account at a different bank and quickly wired the money to complete the property purchase before the banks detected the shortfall. When the first account fell deeply into the negative, prosecutors allege that Luckey used new money raised from venture capital investors to cover the missing funds.Complete loss for venture investorsBy September 2023, the company’s financial problems became impossible to hide. ComplYant faced severe cash shortages, suddenly stopped operating and eventually shut down completely. The collapse left venture capital investors facing total losses on their $13.3 million investments. Prosecutors allege that much of the money had already been spent on company expenses and Luckey’s personal lifestyle, including her Caribbean wedding. The case is being handled by Assistant United States Attorney Andrew M. Roach of the Major Frauds Section in Los Angeles. An indictment is a formal accusation of wrongdoing and does not mean the accused has been found guilty. Federal officials stressed that Luckey is presumed innocent unless and until she is proven guilty in court.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: EU cuts primary student-teacher ratio to 13.3 as decade-long growth falters
articles.summary: The EU had 23.2 million primary students in 2024, down 0.2% from 2023. Since 2014, numbers have risen by 2.9%, though trends vary widely: Luxembourg and Slov...
articles.body:
In 2024, there were 23.2 million primary school students in the European Union, a figure virtually unchanged from the previous year, but the underlying trend has shifted over the past decade: today there are fewer students per teacher than in 2014.

The latest Eurostat data, released to coincide with International Literacy Day, confirm this and not only set out enrolment numbers but also detail how many teachers are in Europe's classrooms, who they are, and what types of schools they work in.

France remains by far the country with the most primary school children: 4.1 million in 2024. It is followed by Germany (3.3 million), Spain (2.8 million) and Italy (2.6 million). At the other end of the scale, Malta has barely 27,537 students; Luxembourg has 43,020, and Cyprus 60,596, figures that depend both on the size of each country and on the age at which children start primary school, which varies from one member state to another.

Compared with last year, overall primary enrolment in the EU fell by 0.2% (35,153 fewer pupils), a small but real drop.

The picture looks different over a longer period: since 2014, pupil numbers have grown by 2.9% (659,086 more), although the trend is highly uneven across countries. Fifteen member states gained pupils over those ten years, and eleven lost them. Luxembourg (+21.4%) and Slovenia (+18.2%) lead the increases; Poland (-25.7%), Croatia (-10.3%), and Portugal (-10.0%) record the largest declines.

The student-teacher ratio in primary schools has fallen since 2014

The student-teacher ratio, an indirect measure of teaching resources in an education system, also shows change. In 2024, the EU average was 13.3 pupils per primary teacher, compared with 14.2 a decade earlier. Greece (7.4) and Luxembourg (8.2) are the only countries below 10; at the other end, Germany (15.2), the Netherlands (16.3), Czechia and France (both 17.9) and Romania (18.2) all have more than 15 pupils per teacher.

The downward trend was repeated in 23 of the 27 countries between 2014 and 2024, with Bulgaria (from 17.8 to 10.4) and Slovenia (from 15.9 to 10.8) showing the sharpest drops. Austria is the exception that proves the rule: its ratio did not shift by a single decimal point, stuck at 12.0. The remaining countries saw increases, and Lithuania saw the most marked change, rising from 10.2 to 13.7 pupils per teacher.

Eurostat also sets out, in a broader analysis of the primary phase, how many teachers stand behind those students. In 2024, there were nearly 1.9 million primary teachers in the EU. Germany tops the list with 284,000, followed by Italy (251,000), Spain (248,000) and France (242,000, an incomplete figure as it does not include independent private schools).

Teaching remains an overwhelmingly female profession: 85.6% of primary teachers in the EU are women, compared with 14.4% men. In nine countries, the male share is below 10%; the most extreme case is Lithuania, where only 3.9% of teachers are men. Denmark, at 32.8%, has the highest male presence in primary classrooms, though males remain a minority.

By age, 42.1% of European teachers are between 35 and 49, 38.1% are over 50, and only 19.7% are under 35. Italy (58.2%) and Lithuania (57.3%) have the oldest staff; Malta and Luxembourg, by contrast, have more than double the EU average share of young teachers.

articles.title: Spain's spy agency warned of Ceuta border breach plans before crisis, declassified files show
articles.summary: Spain's national intelligence agency issued multiple warnings about a potential mass crossing of migrants from Morocco into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta, dec...
articles.body:
Madrid — Spain's national intelligence agency issued multiple warnings before the Ceuta border crisis about a potential mass crossing of migrants from Morocco into the Spanish exclave in late July, according to declassified documents released by the government on Wednesday.

The trove of 40 documents, which includes alerts, intelligence reports, charts and communications from multiple law enforcement and intelligence agencies, appears to undermine what Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has said about the level of warning the government had before the sudden influx took place.

There have been major protests in Spain in response to the migrant arrivals, with critics blaming the Sánchez government for its handling of the crisis, and his political opponents accusing him of pandering to Morocco.

On July 29, a day before more than 72,000 people began pouring into the Spanish city neighboring Morocco, Spain's spy agency, the National Intelligence Center (CNI), sent an alert via WhatsApp to the Spanish government's delegation in Ceuta about calls on social media "for an assault on the fence and by sea tomorrow at 8 p.m."

"There are two different groups with a total of 180,000 followers," the declassified WhatsApp message from the intelligence agency said, "just to give you an idea of its scale."

A report from Spain's spy agency sent that day to Moroccan intelligence services warned of plans on social media for migrants to enter Ceuta on July 30 by climbing a border fence separating the exclave from Morocco, or by swimming around it, the documents show. It mentioned that migrants might take advantage of Morocco's national Throne Day, celebrated on July 30.

That same day, Spain's national intelligence agency issued similar warnings about "several groups on Facebook and WhatsApp encouraging these attempts" in messages to Spain's Civil Guard police force.

Once thousands of people were streaming across the border on July 30, a Defense Ministry intelligence report issued that day stated that Moroccan forces were passive and acted negligently to stop migrants.

"It cannot be ruled out that Morocco may attempt to exploit the situation that has arisen in Ceuta to further its strategic interests," the report went on.

Morocco's foreign ministry didn't immediately respond to a request for comment from The Associated Press about the documents.

On Wednesday, Sánchez rejected the idea that the declassified documents revealed that there was prior warning about a border crisis of the scale that took place between July 30 and 31.

"The existence of this campaign was known ... and was being monitored, but in no way did it constitute or could it be interpreted as an indicator of the scale, nature, or probability of what happened afterward," Sánchez wrote on X, referencing the spy agency's July 29 warning about what was brewing on social media .

Sánchez has defended his government's handling of the crisis and said last week there was no evidence that Morocco's government orchestrated the incident. That sparked further criticism, particularly after a leaked police report alleged the involvement of Moroccan police in the episode.

Several weeks after the initial border rush, Ceuta is dealing with a prolonged humanitarian crisis because of some 5,000 migrants who remain in the small city, according to the national government. Local officials cite a higher figure of up to 10,000 people.

They include unaccompanied minors, the Reuters news agency notes, adding migrants are living in makeshift camps or on Ceuta's streets and beaches, according to local authorities.

The Spanish leader pledged last week to release documents related to Spain's deadliest mass crossing, in which NGOs reported that more than 140 migrants died.

In the days immediately before the mass crossing, hundreds of migrants had swum from Morocco to reach Ceuta, which Spain's Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska acknowledged at the time.

He said authorities were facing "an extraordinary, exceptional situation," and that the Spanish government was "dealing with it with the means that we already have deployed there permanently."

Wednesday's document trove includes reports from multiple agencies that detailed the increasing number of arrivals, a surge that overwhelmed authorities beginning July 30.

articles.title: Ladakh groups express disappointment over MHA meet; Wangchuk warns of fresh stir from Sept 19
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Ladakh groups have expressed disappointment after a meeting with the ministry of home affairs sub-committee, saying the Centre failed to pr.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Ladakh groups have expressed disappointment after a meeting with the ministry of home affairs sub-committee, saying the Centre failed to present the much-awaited draft for a proposed elected body for the Union Territory.Climate activist and Leh Apex Body (LAB) member Sonam Wangchuk said there had been “no special progress” since the May 22 meeting, while Kargil Democratic Alliance (KDA) representative Sajjad Kargili said the delegation had come to Delhi expecting a draft detailing the structure and powers of the proposed body.What are the demands?The LAB and KDA have been seeking an elected legislative body at the UT level and safeguards for land, jobs, culture and identity since talks with the Centre began in 2021, news agency PTI reported.Kargili said the meeting reiterated that the proposed body would be elected, with separate delimitation and constituencies. However, the groups said there was still no clarity on the overall distribution of powers, including law and order.The groups also pressed for early legislation and elections.Wangchuk also mentioned that Centre indicated that compensation would be provided to those killed or injured during the September 24, 2025 violence in Leh and that an announcement was expected soon.“We demanded that all cases should be withdrawn together. They said they will think about it,” Wangchuk said, adding that the delegation could not say the Centre had agreed to the demand.Wangchuk warns of fresh agitationWangchuk has warned that the groups could resume agitation if major decisions were taken before an elected democratic body was established."Will launch a fresh stir from September 19 to 24 over Ladakh issues if we don't get any assurance from the government," he said.The next meeting is likely to be held in Kargil in the first week of October, he said.Ladakh was made a Union Territory without a legislature in 2019. The May 22 talks had resulted in an in-principle understanding on an elected UT-level body and a customised constitutional safeguards framework under Article 371.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.summary: US News: An Indian national of Gujarati origin has pleaded guilty to his role in a multi-million-dollar illegal gambling conspiracy that allegedly operated thr.
articles.body: An Indian national of Gujarati origin has pleaded guilty to his role in a multi-million-dollar illegal gambling conspiracy that allegedly operated through six businesses in southwest Missouri, generating nearly USD 9.36 million (approximately Rs 89 crore) in gross proceeds.Sunilkumar N Patel, 53, a New York resident, pleaded guilty in federal court in Missouri to charges including conspiracy to commit wire fraud, conspiracy to operate an illegal gambling business, conspiracy to commit money laundering, and money laundering, according to the US Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Missouri.Six Missouri locationsPatel admitted that he and his co-conspirators collectively obtained about USD 9,362,114 through the wire fraud scheme and illegal gambling businesses and later carried out financial transactions to launder the proceeds, the US Attorney’s Office said.The operation allegedly ran under the guise of “internet amusement arcade games, skill game arcades, and adult arcades”. Prosecutors said the businesses instead operated contests of chance, gambling devices, and slot machines in violation of Missouri and federal laws.The six locations included four businesses in Springfield - Big Win Arcade #1, Big Win Arcade #2, Spin Hitters and Vegas Arcade. The other two were Spin Zone in Joplin and Vegas City Arcade in Branson West.Patel and his co-conspirators also hired local employees to work at the businesses, according to the US Attorney’s Office.Patel among nine chargedPatel was among nine people charged in a 72-count superseding indictment returned by a federal grand jury in Springfield, Missouri, on May 14, 2025.The indictment alleged that the group operated the businesses between July 1, 2022, and May 13, 2025. All nine defendants were charged with conspiracy to commit wire fraud, conspiracy to operate an illegal gambling business, and operating illegal gambling businesses.All nine also faced at least one count of wire fraud, while eight were charged with money laundering.Patel pleaded guilty before US Chief Magistrate Judge Willie J Epps Jr. He faces up to 20 years in federal prison for conspiracy to commit wire fraud, up to 20 years for conspiracy to operate an illegal gambling business, up to five years for conspiracy to commit money laundering, and up to 20 years each for the money laundering and wire fraud-related counts, according to the US Attorney’s Office.Federal law sets the maximum sentences, while the court will determine the actual sentence based on federal sentencing guidelines and other statutory factors.A sentencing date will be set after a pre-sentence investigation by the US Probation Office.Several federal, state, and local agencies investigated the case, including the FBI, Homeland Security Investigations, IRS-Criminal Investigations, and police departments in Springfield and Joplin.The case is being prosecuted by Assistant US Attorney Casey Clark.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Why the far-right is accusing British lifeboat volunteers of treason
articles.summary: Early September can be a challenging period for Britain’s coastguards as beachgoers try to stretch out the last days of the summer season.
articles.body: Early September can be a challenging period for Britain’s coastguards as beachgoers try to stretch out the last days of the summer season. But this year an unlikely new obstacle stands in the way of lifeboat volunteers working along England’s southern coastline: the far-right. Volunteers from the UK’s Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI), a largely donation-funded charity, have faced a torrent of abuse in recent days, as well as allegations of treason, after helping migrants to safety over the weekend amid major anti-immigration protests. Peter Sparkes, the organization’s CEO, said such abuse was “wholly unacceptable in a civilised society,” and vowed to continue helping “whoever needs our help.” The backlash comes as anti-immigrant sentiments bubble to the surface in some parts of the country – despite the number of migrants crossing the English Channel in small boats falling to its lowest level since 2020, according to the Home Office. Hundreds of balaclava-wearing protesters clashed with police on Sunday night in the coastal city of Portsmouth, southern England, after a small boat carrying migrants was brought into Langstone Harbour. A similar protest unfolded in Dover on Saturday, with groups of masked men dressed in black shouting “stop the boats.” In Portsmouth, a group of far-right agitators first attempted to stop lifeboats from bringing the migrants onshore before seeking to block buses from taking the asylum seekers to a processing facility. The protest appeared to be organized by a group called the Patriot Platform, led by Daniel Thomas, a former associate of the anti-Islamic, far-right political activist Tommy Robinson. British Policing Minister Sarah Jones said Monday that the RNLI acted “under the direction” of the British coastguard to meet the boat, which was carrying approximately 120 people, and take it into the Portsmouth area. “A group of more than 200 protesters arrived at the harbour, intending to block three coaches which were due to take the arrivals for processing,” Jones said. As a result of the RNLI’s involvement, its staff have faced a wave of online abuse and, in the worst cases, physical abuse, according to the organization, with posts on social media calling them “traitors.” “These two helped facilitate the invasion of Britain last night,” one social media user posted on X, while sharing images of RNLI volunteers. “I don’t know how they can look themselves in the mirror.” Rumors are also being spread that asylum seekers are being housed on RNLI premises, something the organization has dismissed as “completely baseless and untrue.” “Recent events have generated deliberate misinformation and a misunderstanding about the RNLI – our purpose, our tasking, and particularly our lifesaving work in the Channel,” Sparkes said. Volunteers have been told they can choose not to wear RNLI branded clothing when representing the charity in public if it makes them feel safer, according to the BBC. “No one who is putting themselves in harm’s way – in which to save lives – should be subject to any level of abuse, and we are working with the RNLI to make sure they are supported,” a Downing Street spokesperson said. A very small percentage of RNLI’s total rescue work is focused on the English Channel, according to Sparkes, with most migrants rescued in the area picked up by the UK Border Force. “Illegal immigration is a political issue; the RNLI exists to save lives at sea,” he said on Tuesday. “We will always answer the call, whoever needs our help.”

articles.title: Salvation Army responder opens up on 9/11 cancer battle, phone call that changed his life
articles.summary: Salvation Army responder Ken Tregellas battled stage 4 cancer after months at Ground Zero but says he wouldn't have changed a thing about serving.
articles.body: Twenty-five years later, the grief of Sept. 11 remains with Salvation Army responder Ken Tregellas, and so does his conviction that his experience was worth the sacrifice. "My kids had asked me over the years, ‘Dad, knowing you'd get cancer, would you still have served?’ And I told them, ‘I wouldn't have changed a thing. It was an honor,’" he said. During this year's anniversary, Tregellas is looking back on the decision that took him from his family in Wisconsin to Ground Zero, where he spent months caring for people searching for answers about their loved ones. It started as a typical Tuesday morning. Tregellas was getting his twins ready for school when he saw the North Tower had been struck. Like millions of Americans, he was confused. It wasn't until United Flight 175 struck the second tower that he knew America was under attack. SCIENTISTS DISCOVER POSSIBLE LINK BETWEEN 9/11 AND ACCELERATED AGING Within a few hours, his phone rang, a call that would change the course of his life. Tregellas previously operated The Salvation Army's emergency assistance programs in underserved communities. So when he was asked to be the Red Zone coordinator at Ground Zero, he knew he needed to deploy. When flights opened back up, Tregellas flew from Wisconsin to New York City. Only four other passengers were on board. "I'd never been to New York in my life, so I really didn't have, other than pictures and movies, I didn't have anything to compare it to," he said. Tregellas could not have known that his first glimpse of New York would come under such unimaginable circumstances. Walking into the Red Zone in Lower Manhattan, he encountered a scene unlike anything he had ever witnessed. Smoke continued to rise from the twisted shards of metal, while the remains of the World Trade Center smoldered in a massive pile. "I was still pretty shocked that there was still fire burning," Tregellas said. "I mean, the piles where the two main towers were, were still burning every time they were picking up debris." Working at Ground Zero As the Red Zone coordinator, Tregellas was responsible for overseeing all of The Salvation Army's efforts on the ground. "Our job was really to take care of the people that were looking for bodies at that point," Tregellas said. "It was more of a recovery effort." Six tents were set up at the site, including makeshift cafeterias and sleeping areas that quickly became a refuge for workers. Weary responders arrived with boots melted by the intense heat of the metal. They could replace their shoes, grab a meal, rest and talk with others about what they had witnessed at the pile. The Salvation Army provided more than food, clothing and shelter. Beyond basic necessities, workers received counseling and other forms of spiritual relief to make the grueling work at Ground Zero somewhat manageable. Tregellas emphasized that the organization's mission went beyond meeting physical needs. It was also there to provide emotional and spiritual care. 9/11 VICTIM'S IDENTITY EMERGES NEARLY 25 YEARS LATER AFTER DNA BREAKTHROUGH CRACKS MYSTERY Prayer was offered around the clock to anyone who wanted it. Tregellas said one of the most striking parts of the experience was the diversity of people who came to the site including families who traveled from around the world searching for answers about their loved ones. "There were people coming from all over the world to look at the site and try to understand why they weren't hearing anything about loved ones," Tregellas said. "You had to listen. You were dealing with interpreters. It was a whole different thing than I think most of us had ever dealt with before." At Ground Zero, Tregellas said, the work extended far beyond recovery. The Salvation Army was caring for people in the middle of unimaginable loss, providing a meal, a place to rest, a prayer or simply someone willing to listen. The weight of recovery Although he had worked for The Salvation Army for almost 32 years and witnessed many heartbreaking moments, the weight of what Tregellas witnessed at Ground Zero followed him home. After seeing the scale of the loss in New York, he found himself struggling to process other disasters the way he once had. Returning to disaster sites, such as floods, where people had lost their homes and belongings, he found himself comparing those losses to the lives lost on Sept. 11. "Seeing the depth of tragedy of New York, so much loss of life, and just how large and devastating it was, I really had a hard time on the empathy part," Tregellas said. He knew the loss of a home, furniture or clothing was devastating to the people experiencing it. But privately, he found himself thinking about how different those losses were from what he had witnessed in New York. "I was thinking in my head, ‘that's just stuff, you didn't lose your life," he said. "And I compared everything in my life, even my children I would tell them, doesn't compare to the loss of life. I had a really hard time getting over that." Lingering effect of 9/11 Cancer certifications have risen from 3,204 in 2015 to 57,044 this year between workers, Twin Tower survivors, and Manhattan residents, The New York Post reports. Ten years after Sept. 11, Tregellas became a part of those statistics. When Tregellas was having trouble eating and swallowing, he went to the doctor, not thinking much of it and unaware that his sacrifice helping others at Ground Zero would come at a cost. During the visit, doctors found cancer in his tonsils. "I hadn't really dealt with cancer at all. And then as they started to look at it and it showed up in a couple other places," he said. FRANK SILLER: 'I LOVE YOU, BROTHER' -- THE 9/11 LOSS THAT INSPIRED A MISSION OF SERVICE He was then diagnosed with stage 4 mantle B-cell lymphoma, and the treatment was intense. "It was probably eight months of chemotherapy and long stays in the hospital, and it was a very rare cancer." According to the Victims Compensation Fund, cancer has become one of the lingering health consequences of 9/11, as responders and survivors continue to face illnesses linked to their exposure at Ground Zero. There were more than 69 reported types of cancer, with non-melanoma skin cancer being the most common, with more than 18,400 cases among responders and survivors, while lymphoma, on the rarer side, accounted for around 2,500 cases among responders and survivors. The 9/11 VCF was able to assist him with his treatment. "I went through a bunch of chemotherapies. I had a stem cell transplant that was, they said, my best chance to survive." About a year after completing that first treatment, the cancer came back in his other tonsil. "I thought we were just going to do the same thing again, which I wasn't excited about, but I was thinking, ‘Well, it worked once, it can work again,’" he said. Doctors thought that would be too harsh on his body, so they put him on ibrutinib, a drug used to treat certain blood cancers and one he’d be on until this year. "And boy, I was on that drug till February of this year, and it put me back in remission, I never had any cancer since," he said. Keeping the memory alive Today, Tregellas spends part of his time speaking, often to students, about what he witnessed on 9/11. For many of them, the attacks are something they have only learned about in history books. When speaking to Fox News, he got emotional. He took a beat with a heavy sigh that held weight as if sharing his experiences with younger generations brought him back in time to those moments. Tregellas knows he and others on the ground will never forget. But feels it’s vital to bring it to the forefront so the younger generations know, so they can remember. "That's where we bring it back," Tregella said. "It's an important part of history. And yeah, it united us. I think it still does at times." This week, on the 25th anniversary, he says most of all he looks forward to the shared solidarity. "And yeah, I'm proud to be a part of that."

articles.title: Prince Harry, Bill Nye, Chrissy Teigen to join this year’s Clinton Global Initiative meeting
articles.summary: Former President Clinton and former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton are tapping Prince Harry, World Bank Group President Ajay Banga, TV personality and entrepreneur Chrissy Teigen, LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman and celebrity science educator Bill Nye for this year’s Clinton Global Initiative annual meeting. The lineup for the yearly gathering in New York — scheduled…
articles.body:
Former President Clinton and former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton are tapping Prince Harry, World Bank Group President Ajay Banga, TV personality and entrepreneur Chrissy Teigen, LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman and celebrity science educator Bill Nye for this year’s Clinton Global Initiative annual meeting.

The lineup for the yearly gathering in New York — scheduled for Sept. 22-23, during the United Nations General Assembly week — was announced Thursday.

“This year’s meeting is organized around the theme ‘How Do We Get It Right?’, charting out an affirmative vision for the future amidst rising turmoil, division, and continued cuts to government funding,” the organization, founded by the 42nd president in 2005, said in a news release.

It’s not the first time that Harry — who recently made headlines for returning to the U.K. with his family after living for six years in California — has served as a Clinton Global Initiative meeting headliner. In 2024, the British royal family member spoke at the event and warned of an “epidemic” among young people created by social media platforms that he described as “designed to create addiction.”

Nye and Banga have also previously participated in the Clintons’ annual summit.

According to the Clinton Global Initiative, issues on this year’s agenda include “mitigating the risks” of artificial intelligence and “driving innovation,” climate and energy resilience, democracy and “what it takes to rebuild trust, safeguard civic institutions and protect journalists when headlines and algorithms constantly emphasize our differences,” as well as humanitarian response efforts, economic opportunities and health and “sustaining research and innovation at a moment when funding and trust are both under strain.”

Other participants announced Thursday include Nobel Peace laureate Muhammad Yunus, United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees and former Iraqi President Barham Salih, Octopus Energy Group CEO Greg Jackson, content creator Aaron Parnas, and Omidyar Network CEO Michele Jawando.
