articles.title: 9/11 hero Welles Crowther's firehouse president reveals what shaped the 'man in the red bandana'
articles.summary: Welles Crowther's volunteer firehouse shaped the hero who saved 18 lives on 9/11. Its president reveals how training and community forged the legend.
articles.body: When President Donald Trump awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom posthumously to Welles Crowther for his heroism during the 9/11 terrorist attack during a Tuesday ceremony, Crowther's mother Alison specifically mentioned the Upper Nyack, New York, volunteer firehouse where Welles got his training. "Welles... would not have been able to do what he did as effectively on 9/11 if it had not been for the training and experience he gained as a member of Empire Hook and Ladder Company Number One of Upper Nyack," she said. Crowther, as Empire Hook and Ladder Company Number One president David "Trevor" Gottlieb explained to Fox News Digital, was forged in the volunteer firehouse's traditions of community and sacrifice. FIRST ON FOX: TRUMP’S 9/11 TRIBUTE TO FEATURE MASSIVE PIECE OF GROUND ZERO HISTORY AT WHITE HOUSE "I joined in '88, he was five years younger than me so probably '93 is when he first started," Gottlieb told Fox News Digital. "I was still away in college. I came back and worked with him from '93 on. Volunteer fire service is usually multi-generational, and Welles' father, Jefferson, was an ex-captain. He was our treasurer, just, you know, part of the fabric of the company. Kid's been coming down here since he could walk," Gottlieb said. In the 25 years since the terrorist attacks on 9/11, Crowther's story has become something of a legend. Known as the "man in the red bandana," Crowther carried a red bandana on his wallet while working as a stockbroker in the South Tower. When the attack struck, he immediately leapt to action, helping usher people to safety as the building burned around him. "Welles Crowther was in the towers. He was working for a trading firm that day. And he assisted with the rescue of at least 18, I think was the final count they got. Eighteen civilians that he helped lead to safety and ultimately lost his life doing that," Gottlieb said. "I think what Welles' impression he left upon us was anything's possible. And when you're faced with, you know, 108 floors and the chaos and the destruction all around you, when you sit back and rely on your training, on how you were brought up, I think that makes your job much easier," he continued. Gottlieb credited Crowther's instinct to help people without hesitation to his upbringing at Empire Hook and Ladder. "This fire company is stocked with great people. We have five generations, some of the families go back in this company. And it's great to see the pride, the dedication, commitment to a community that exists when you have such a special place like this," he said. "I would lay my life down for any one of them. And I think they would do the same for me," Gottlieb said of his firehouse family. "That's something that's kind of instilled in when you join here. And it's perfected throughout years and multi-generations of that behavior," he continued. 9/11 MUSEUM UNVEILS EXHIBITION FOR GENERATION TOO YOUNG TO REMEMBER THE ATTACKS: 'CALLED EVERYBODY TO LEAD' Crowther's ultimate sacrifice was indicative not only of his upbringing in Empire Hook and Ladder, but of the spirit that inhabits all volunteer firefighters, Gottlieb argued. "When you look at what happened that day, somebody made the decision to not run. They made the decision to stay and help. And they didn't ask if you're a Republican, a Democrat, a Muslim, a Jew, a Catholic," he told Fox News Digital. "You're somebody who needs help. And the human spirit needs to continue that way. We have to focus on what brings us together, not what divides us," Gottlieb said. "And I think that's been kind of the driving force in the firehouse. For us to get more volunteers, we can't be a polarizing organization. We can't have sides. Our position is we're here to help the community." "We are here to step up in the times that probably matter most and be part of something much bigger than ourselves," he added. "And when you learn to set that aside and you learn to live with those kinds of principles, I think it makes this job much easier because you know that – know – the guy next to you, the girl next to has your back and I have their back." NYPD CHIEF: 9/11 HEROES’ LEGACY LIVES ON IN EVERY GENERATION OF OFFICERS Gottlieb also pointed to two of Empire's other fallen firefighters, Harry Wannamaker Jr. and Joe Stach Jr., who he said both lost their lives due to health complications related to 9/11. "We should never forget. We should never forget the sacrifice that everybody made, in particular Welles. But there was 343 other firemen that died. And then, since that time, we've lost two more members in Empire related to 9/11 diseases, Harry Wanamaker Jr. and Joe Stach Jr. And it's awful to see the scars that it leaves on families forever," he said. MASSACHUSETTS TOWN CANCELS JULY 4 CELEBRATION CITING LACK OF 'ADEQUATE PUBLIC SAFETY STAFFING' Gottlieb also urged people to follow in Crowther's footsteps and volunteer for their local fire departments. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Volunteer fire service is hurting for people right now. Everybody's too busy to volunteer and I can't describe to you the feeling, right? You get to drive fire trucks, you get to play with some pretty cool tools. I encourage everyone to do this, make time, help any way you can because your community will be better for it," he said.

articles.title: Princess Diana’s ‘revenge dress’ is going up for auction
articles.summary: Princess Diana’s head-turning “revenge dress,” which broke royal protocol and created a sensational pop culture moment, is going on sale for the first time in nearly 30 years.
articles.body: Princess Diana’s head-turning “revenge dress,” which broke royal protocol and created a sensational pop culture moment, is going on sale for the first time in nearly 30 years. The showstopping evening gown by Greek designer Christina Stambolian will be exhibited in London this month, before heading to Hong Kong, Geneva, and finally New York, where it is expected to sell for up to $300,000 when it goes under the hammer on December 9. The late Princess of Wales wore the black, figure-hugging dress on June 29, 1994 — the same day that her then-husband, now-King Charles III, admitted in an ITN documentary that he’d been unfaithful. The revelation had been leaked days prior by the British press and the documentary aired to 13 million viewers nationwide. Yet Diana chose to arrive for a party at the Serpentine Gallery in London in a gown so captivating it received its own moniker, becoming known as “the revenge dress.” Pairing the shoulder-baring silk design with black heels, a black clutch, bold red nails and a jeweled chocker – created from an antique diamond and sapphire brooch that Queen Elizabeth, the Queen Mother, gifted her for her wedding, according to Sotheby’s – Diana reclaimed her image in the public’s imagination. “Fashion can be a language when words fail or are simply not enough. Princess Diana understood that instinctively,” said Morgane Halimi, head of handbags and fashion at Sotheby’s, in a statement Thursday. “On her own terms, Princess Diana turned the dress into one of the most powerful messages she ever made, during one of the most scrutinised and emotionally charged episodes of her life,” Halimi added. At the time, black was only considered appropriate for royals during funerals. Stambolian’s design is a version of the little black dress, a fashion statement first conceived in 1926 by Coco Chanel to reimagine black, from a color of mourning to one of sophisticated chic, and free women from the fashion constraint of earlier times, according to Sotheby’s. Diana made the impulsive decision to wear the black design, which had been sitting in her closet for three years out of fear it was “too daring,” Stambolian said in the 2013 Channel 4 documentary “Princess Diana’s Dresses: The Auction.” The dark outfit and its pop culture moment has since been memorialized in clothing lines, on social media and on TV programs such as Netflix’s historical drama “The Crown.” “What became a global viral moment – long before social media made the term mundane – also gave license to anyone, but especially women, to use fashion beyond adornment and much more intentionally and meaningfully: as a shield, a weapon or both,” Halimi said. “What has endured across the decades is not the scandal surrounding that evening, but Princess Diana’s show of confidence and self-possession,” Halimi added. ‘Something special’ Diana “wanted to look a million dollars” when she stepped out in the dress, according to the stylist that helped her get ready, Anna Harvey, Sotheby’s said. Considering one of Diana’s less famous dresses far exceeded estimates in 2023, selling for $604,800, this dress could hold more value than estimated. After all, Diana’s famous “black sheep” sweater broke records in 2023 when it sold for more than $1.1 million. The “revenge dress” was last sold in June 1997, when Diana auctioned 79 of her dresses to raise funds for breast cancer and AIDS charities, Sotheby’s said. It then appeared at charity fundraiser events in Scotland before it was last seen on display at the country’s Paisley Museum nearly three decades ago. A rare copy of the catalogue from the original sale – which credits Prince William with the sale’s design and which was signed by the late princess and the dress designer – will be sold with the gown. “My late husband and I knew that this dress was something special,” said the anonymous consignor who bought the dress in 1997. “Princess Diana was walking into the worst night of her life and you would never know it to look at her. It went from a cocktail dress to a statement in the time it took to photograph her.” “Thirty years on, you can say the words anywhere in the world and everyone knows exactly which dress you mean,” they added. “I hope it goes to someone who will enjoy owning it as much as we did.” Some of the proceeds from the sale will be donated to health service charity NHS Lothian Charity, according to the auction house. The dress will be unveiled at Sotheby’s London on September 18 and displayed until September 24, before exhibiting in Hong Kong from October 1 to 15, in Geneva from November 6 to 11, and in New York from December 2.

articles.title: Trump says ‘no damage’ to US war planes from Iran attack
articles.summary: President Trump on Thursday denied reports that Iranian forces damaged U.S. war planes during a raid on an air base in Jordan. “Nope,” the president said when NewsNation’s Robert Sherman asked whether there is “any truth” to the reports. “None whatsoever. No damage. No nothing,” Trump told Sherman over the phone. CBS News, citing people…
articles.body:
President Trump on Thursday denied reports that Iranian forces damaged U.S. war planes during a raid on an air base in Jordan.

“Nope,” the president said when NewsNation’s Robert Sherman asked whether there is “any truth” to the reports.

“None whatsoever. No damage. No nothing,” Trump told Sherman over the phone.

CBS News, citing people with direct knowledge of the matter, reported Thursday that Iranian strikes damaged multiple American military aircraft overnight Tuesday into Wednesday.

The strikes occurred during an attack on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan, which the Royal Jordanian Air Force operates.

One A-10 Thunderbolt lost a wing in the attack, while roughly eight F-15s sustained light damage and returned to service, CBS News reported.

Iranian forces launched ballistic missiles toward the base in response to the U.S. military destroying five Iranian oil tankers Tuesday.

The Iran conflict, in its seven month, has marched on with no sign of a deal to end hostilities. Trump told Sherman the war will “get settled right after” the U.S. midterm elections in November.

“They can’t hold out any longer,” the president told reporters at Joint Base Andrews on Wednesday, referring to Iran. “They’re desperate to try and affect the election so that we can get a nice, weak group of people in there, and leave them alone and let them have their nuclear weapon.”

Trump also said he is “not looking for” negotiations with Iranian officials to resume, adding of the Islamic Republic, “We have very little country left.”

The president remarked, “Yes, a negotiation could possibly happen, but it’s not something we’re looking at.”

The war has depleted the Pentagon’s stockpiles of critical munitions . As of July 27, the U.S. military had used up roughly two-thirds of its stockpile of Patriot missile interceptors and more than half of its Terminal High Altitude Area Defense systems, according to analysts at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

articles.title: Former President Bush to Gen. Dan Caine: ‘Thank God you are where you are’
articles.summary: Former President George W. Bush on Thursday lavished praise on Joint Chiefs of Staff Chair Gen. Dan Caine, amid the ongoing war with Iran. “Thank God you are where you are, and we appreciate it,” Bush said to Caine during an event commemorating the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. The former president,…
articles.body:
Former President George W. Bush on Thursday lavished praise on Joint Chiefs of Staff Chair Gen. Dan Caine, amid the ongoing war with Iran .

“Thank God you are where you are, and we appreciate it,” Bush said to Caine during an event commemorating the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.

The former president, who was in office the day of the attacks, made the remarks while speaking with his former Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice from his presidential center at Southern Methodist University in Dallas.

A trained F-16 fighter pilot, Caine was among the pilots who patrolled Washington, D.C., airspace in the aftermath of 9/11 and later served in the Bush White House.

Now President Trump’s principal military adviser, Caine reportedly warned the president before the start of the Iran war that the U.S.’s limited stockpile of critical munitions and little to no support from allies would put military personnel in danger and hamper a large-scale operation.

And over the past few months, Caine has reportedly told other top Trump advisers that Washington needs to end the conflict soon as escalating the war via the U.S. military is likely to backfire.

Trump on Wednesday for the first time acknowledged that the deeply unpopular war, now in its seventh month, will not be resolved until after the November midterm elections.

“I think the war is going to end immediately after the election,” he told reporters at Joint Base Andrews en route to the GOP midterm convention in Dallas.

He accused Iran of trying to meddle in the elections, saying “they’re desperate to try and affect the election so that we can get a nice, weak group of people in there, and leave them alone and let them have their nuclear weapon.”

Trump has also pressured Tehran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and remains adamant that the regime cannot obtain a nuclear weapon. But the conflict is at a stalemate after multiple attempts at peace talks have failed.

The president has also repeatedly asserted all options remain on the table to push Tehran, including further military action.

articles.title: The House must act to cut Putin’s Arctic gas lifeline
articles.summary: The bipartisan Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act passed the Senate, potentially allowing the U.S. government to block the specialized tankers used by Russia to export liquefied natural gas from the Yamal peninsula to Europe.
articles.body:
On Siberia’s edge, cranes rise from tundra at Sabetta on the Yamal Peninsula . From there, tankers carry Russian gas out of the Arctic towards European ports and shipyards.

One is the Boris Davydov, which carried gas from Yamal to Dunkirk before sailing to Denmark for servicing at the Fayard shipyard. Once maintenance ends, it can begin the journey again.

Follow the ship and a whole system becomes visible. Foreign-owned tankers carry gas through the Arctic. European ports that receive them. European shipyards keep them operating. Each stage depends on support beyond Russia.

Yamal’s size disguises a narrow weakness: The project relies on specially designed 14 tankers that can force their way through Arctic ice when other carriers cannot. Without access to this fleet, its winter exports would halt almost entirely.

Russia has reopened Arctic sites and ports and expanded cooperation with China along the Northern Sea Route. Yamal is part of the infrastructure. Putin launched its first tanker in 2017 as evidence of Russia’s growing Arctic power. Every cargo delivered and every tanker repaired helps turn that ambition into a full-blown export system.

Europe has become Yamal’s main destination. During the first six months of 2026, European Union ports received 136 of its 140 cargoes . Those deliveries totaled 9.97 million tons and had an estimated gross value of €5.96 billion.

Americans may ask why Washington should address a trade that Europe finances. In its 21st sanctions package, the EU maintained its planned import ban for pipeline gas but created an exemption for Russian liquefied natural gas. The exemption preserves a commercial role for qualifying European companies, one of which operates five of Yamal’s 14 tankers . It runs until July 25, 2027, then continues for successive one-year periods unless the European Council decides otherwise after an annual review.

Legislation championed by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) could change the calculation. Graham spent more than a year building support for stronger sanctions and secured White House agreement shortly before his death.

The bipartisan Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act passed the Senate 86-11 on Aug. 7 . President Trump supports it, but the House has not yet scheduled a vote .

The bill names Yamal and the Arctic 1, 2 and 3 liquefied natural gas projects. It requires the president to review covered vessels within 30 days of enactment and block any he determines meets its criteria. The 14 tankers moving Russian gas into Europe offer a defined fleet for review.

The House should pass Graham’s legislation with its Arctic provisions intact. If enacted, the administration should use the 30-day review to examine every Arc7 tanker serving Yamal and coordinate action with Europe, Britain and other allies.

Without action, the Boris Davydov will leave Denmark once again, return to Yamal and load again. Another tanker will follow. Congress can interrupt that journey, weaken Putin’s flagship project and show that Moscow cannot write the commercial rules of the Arctic alone.

Alexander Kirk is senior campaign manager and strategic communications advisor at Urgewald, where he works on sanctions and Russian energy.

articles.title: Use all powers necessary on anti-migrant protests, home secretary tells police
articles.summary: Two anti-migrant protests took place in Dover and Portsmouth last weekend.
articles.body:
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has told police chiefs that lessons must be learned from how they handled last weekend's anti-migrant protests in Dover and Portsmouth - saying she expects officers to use all powers necessary.

In a meeting on Thursday she asked for reassurance that plans were in place for the police to move quickly and effectively in dealing with far-right groups seeking to intimidate communities.

It comes after masked activists brought Dover to a standstill on Saturday and in a protest on Sunday in Portsmouth about 200 people tried to block migrants being driven away for processing.

In a summary of the meeting, the Home Office said the protests brought "unacceptable disorder".

RNLI volunteer targeted online and branded 'traitor' after Portsmouth protests

"These scenes have caused disruption for people and, given that people are dressed in black wearing balaclavas, there is a fear factor and obvious malign intent being communicated to our residents," the Home Secretary said.

"This makes it different from other protests, so we need to make sure we are learning lessons."

The BBC understands that police chiefs are now actively considering using recently-granted powers to completely ban face coverings in specific areas, in light of that demonstration.

Saturday's protest was followed 24 hours later with another in which men blocked the only road out of Langstone Harbour, near Portsmouth, after the RNLI had brought ashore 120 migrants.

It's unclear at this stage whether further such protests will go ahead - but in some areas of England local groups that have associated themselves with the Patriot Platform umbrella group have called for more demonstrations.

The meeting discussed the emergence of Patriot Platform with ministers believing the group aims to intimidate communities.

Mahmood is said to have told police chiefs to make better use of intelligence to make sure they had better plans in place ahead of this weekend.

That call came after Kent Police had earlier admitted it had been made aware of a potential demonstration in Dover but had not "fully assessed" the warning before the town's nationally critical port road was brought to a standstill.

During the meeting, Mahmood is said to have made clear the government expected police to make full use of powers and to deal robustly with any criminal offences.

Speaking after the meeting, Deputy Chief Constable Andy Mariner, the National Police Chiefs Council lead for public order, said forces were "continually assessing and preparing for protests and any potential impact on public safety".

This includes working closely with "local forces, specialist teams, communities and partners" to ensure support is available when needed.

He added: "Our priority is to keep people safe, maintain public order and support the right to peaceful and lawful protest. While people are entitled to express their views, anyone committing criminal offences can and should expect police action."

Major changes to protest law in the last three years mean officers can now intervene more quickly to end demonstrations that block critical national infrastructure, such as roads to ports.

They can also designate an entire area a face mask-free zone for the duration of a protest.

It's that second power that police chiefs are now considering using.

Police chiefs also say they have initiated an "enhanced and co-ordinated" approach to gathering as much intelligence as possible in the days ahead.

articles.title: Iran-backed rebels capture Red Sea port, tightening grip on a key global chokepoint
articles.summary: Iran-backed proxies in Yemen captured strategic locations along the Red Sea on Thursday, potentially expanding Tehran’s influence over another key Middle Eastern waterway.
articles.body: Iran-backed proxies in Yemen captured strategic locations along the Red Sea on Thursday, potentially expanding Tehran’s influence over another key Middle Eastern waterway. On Thursday, the Houthi fighters captured the town of Mocha, a crucial coastal location some 50 miles to the north of Perim, the information minister of the internationally recognized government told CNN. The news sent shockwaves across the world over the potential impact on global shipping. A gateway to the route between Asia and Europe via the Suez Canal, Bab al-Mandeb is a geopolitical chokepoint similar to the Strait of Hormuz linking Asia and Europe via the Suez Canal. While it is less critical to global trade than Hormuz, it still carries essential goods worldwide, including millions of barrels of oil every day. The development coincides with a wider regional escalation of the war between Iran and the United States, after Tehran warned this week that it would step up hostilities against the US, which maintains a stringent naval blockade of Iran and continues to launch military strikes on the country. How did we get here? After years of stalemate, fighting between Saudi-backed forces and Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen flared up again over the past month as a result of tensions caused by the wider regional conflict between Iran and the US. The Red Sea became a focal point as Iran sought ways to pressure the global economy and extract more concessions from Washington. Last month, Tehran’s proxies in Yemen, the Houthis, intensified an offensive to seize the port city of Mocha from Saudi-backed forces. A few weeks ago, more than 25 Houthi rockets slammed into the sprawling harbor as commercial ships were unloading, according to port director Abdel Malek Al-Sharaabi. Until Thursday morning, the city was under the control of the National Resistance Forces, a Saudi-backed group commanded by Tarik Saleh, a vice president in Yemen’s beleaguered internationally recognized government. The Houthis later claimed to have captured it, and reports began emerging that the group is advancing on other cities in a bid to seize the entire coastline. In an exclusive interview with CNN earlier this month, Saleh warned that if the Houthis seized Perim Island – an island lying directly on the Bab al-Mandeb chokepoint – they could gain control of the strait itself. Dislodging them would require “a massive (international) force and the navies,” he said. Why has this happened now? The Houthi offensive to capture key strategic locations along the western coast overlooking the Red Sea achieves two key objectives for the rebels, according to one expert. “They are in a good position to increase their influence around Bab Al-Mandeb…and they can now protect themselves from any ground operations that can come from this area,” Ahmed Nagi, a senior analyst for Yemen with the International Crisis Group, told CNN. Despite the stalemate that has followed the 2022 truce between the Houthis and Saudi-backed forces, tensions had been simmering between the Yemeni factions for months amid severe economic and humanitarian hardship. In July they reached boiling point when the Houthis allowed an Iranian plane – expected to carry a Houthi delegation to the funeral of Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei – to land in the capital, Sanaa. The move directly challenged Saudi-imposed control over Yemeni airspace and prompted retaliation from the kingdom, which ordered strikes on Houthi-controlled runways at Sanaa airport, breaking years of truce. The Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of imposing a blockade and responded by blockading Saudi ships, firing on vessels transiting waters near Yemen, and attacking oil facilities in the kingdom. The strikes also allowed Iran to increase pressure on Saudi Arabia, a US ally that hosts American troops and bases that Tehran says were used to target it. What now? The capture of Mocha could give a group trained and aided by Iran’s Revolutionary Guards greater influence in the Red Sea while expanding its control over more territory in Yemen – although experts note that the front lines keep changing. Beyond its geopolitical impact, the development risks worsening Yemen’s humanitarian crisis, already designated by the United Nations as one of the world’s worst. An effective Houthi blockade of Bab al-Mandeb would open a new front in the war with Iran and could require US military intervention, potentially weakening Washington’s ability to keep ships moving through Hormuz. It could also prevent Saudi Arabia from shipping diesel to Europe at a critical moment for the fuel market. The move also adds further volatility to oil markets, already under pressure from the very low number of vessels transiting Hormuz. Oil prices jumped 4% on Thursday, with global benchmark Brent crude hitting $105, as news broke of the Houthis gaining ground along the Red Sea. Despite the concern, several Houthis officials have signaled that the advancement does not constitute a concern for international maritime shipping. “The question now is how the Saudi-led coalition will react,” Nagi of the Crisis Group said. “This is not the end of the battle, we will probably see more developments in the coming days.”

articles.title: 10 years after Sinjar, the world still fails to protect vulnerable communities
articles.summary: Reflecting on the ten-year anniversary of the ISIS genocide against the Yazidi people in Sinjar, Cudi Zerey argues that true protection requires proactive early action, locally trusted security, political agency for survivors, and sustained reconstruction efforts.
articles.body:
On Aug. 3, 2014, fighters from the so-called Islamic State in Syria and Iraq swept into Sinjar, the ancestral homeland of Iraq’s Yazidi minority. Within days, thousands were killed, thousands more were kidnapped and enslaved, and entire communities were uprooted. The United Nations would later recognize these crimes as genocide . Yet a decade later, the most important lesson of Sinjar remains largely unlearned.

The failure was not simply that ISIS committed atrocities. The failure was that nearly every layer of protection collapsed at the same time. Local security arrangements failed. Political authorities failed. International actors reacted only after mass violence had already begun . And even today, many Yazidis remain displaced , while Sinjar continues to struggle with insecurity, contested governance and insufficient reconstruction.

Too often, policymakers discuss atrocities as if the central challenge is how to respond once the killing starts. Sinjar demonstrates a different reality: By the time emergency intervention becomes necessary, protection has already failed.

This pattern is hardly unique to Iraq. Around the world, vulnerable communities continue to live in fragile environments characterized by weak governance , contested authority, armed competition and rising extremist violence . Far less attention is devoted to preventing vulnerable populations from becoming trapped in catastrophe in the first place. The first lesson from Sinjar is therefore that early warning means little without early action.

Before ISIS captured Sinjar, the group’s ideology, territorial expansion and hostility toward minorities were already widely known. Yet warnings were not translated into effective preventive measures for the Yazidi population. Governments and international organizations frequently produce risk assessments, conflict forecasts and atrocity warnings . But warning systems do not save lives by themselves. Without contingency planning, evacuation mechanisms and clearly defined triggers for preventive action, early warning risks becoming little more than documentation of a future failure.

A second lesson is that protection must be locally legitimate. One of the overlooked dimensions of Sinjar is that security arrangements existed on paper but proved unreliable when tested by crisis. The presence of armed actors is not the same as genuine protection. Vulnerable communities need security institutions they trust and believe will remain committed when violence escalates. In many contemporary conflicts, minority groups are expected to rely on external security guarantees provided by actors whose priorities may change quickly. Protection depends on whether communities believe those troops will act when needed.

The third lesson is that vulnerable communities require political agency, not merely physical protection. The Yazidis were not simply passive victims waiting to be rescued. Like many threatened minorities, they possessed local knowledge and leadership structures. Yet decisions affecting their future were often made by others. Too often, protection policies treat endangered communities as objects of international concern rather than partners in protection. This not only undermines legitimacy but also disregards local knowledge that can strengthen prevention, resilience and recovery.

Justice constitutes a fourth lesson. Accountability remains essential, but justice after atrocity cannot be reduced to criminal prosecutions alone. Survivors need recognition, support, legal protection and opportunities to rebuild their lives . Many Yazidi survivors continue to face the consequences of displacement, trauma and social disruption years after ISIS lost territorial control. If protection ends when the shooting stops, then protection was never truly achieved.

Finally, reconstruction is itself a form of security. A community cannot recover if roads remain unsafe, schools remain closed, public services remain absent and political uncertainty discourages return. The military defeat of a perpetrator does not automatically restore the security of those who suffered from its crimes. For many Yazidis, displacement remains a present reality . Sustainable return requires safety, governance, representation, livelihoods and functioning institutions .

Ten years after Sinjar, remembrance alone is not enough. Every anniversary brings statements of solidarity and promises that such crimes must never happen again. But declarations are easy. Building protection systems that act before communities are abandoned is much harder. The world often measures success by how quickly it responds to atrocities. Sinjar suggests a different standard. Success should be measured by whether vulnerable communities receive protection before mass violence begins, whether they have a voice in decisions affecting their future and whether they can return home safely after conflict ends.

The Yazidi genocide was not only a tragedy of the past. It remains a warning for the future. The lesson of Sinjar is that warning signs are often visible long before mass violence begins. Governments and international organizations already possess many of the tools needed to protect vulnerable communities. What remains missing is the political will to act before catastrophe unfolds. Ten years after Sinjar, preventing the next atrocity will require moving protection from rhetoric to action.

Cudi Zerey is a management consultant specializing in public-sector and defense transformation and a doctoral researcher at the University of Vechta. His research focuses on climate security, resilience, sustainable armed forces, and military transformation.

articles.body: Ryanair CEO Michael O’Leary has disputed a passenger’s claim that he was partially sucked out of a plane after a window shattered mid-flight, saying the man was “certainly sucked towards the window” but never actually went through it. O’Leary made the comments on Thursday as he addressed reporters following Ryanair’s annual general meeting in Dublin, where he said the airline would challenge the passenger’s account while awaiting the outcome of a US investigation into the incident.“He wasn’t partially out the window. Part of his face didn’t get out the window,” O’Leary said. “We don’t think any part of his body got out the window, but he was certainly sucked in very dramatic circumstances towards the window.”On July 10, 61-year-old Serbian businessman Ljubisa Karović, who was travelling on a Ryanair flight from Thessaloniki, Greece, to Memmingen, Germany, was pulled towards the window midair when a window shattered. His wife Svetlana Grković said half of the husband's body was outside the window while she pulled him back inside the aircraft.Karović’s lawyer alleged that a window beside him shattered after debris from the aircraft’s engine struck it, causing sudden depressurisation. According to his legal team, Karović’s head and right arm were pulled towards and partly through the opening. Karović said his seatbelt kept him from being pulled completely out of the aircraft.The passenger reportedly suffered serious neck and shoulder injuries in the incident and was hospitalized.'No part of his body was outside'O’Leary said Karović remained secured in his seat throughout the incident. “He was belted into the seat,” the Ryanair chief said, adding that the airline would “certainly at the end of the process” dispute that the passenger or “any part of his anatomy” went through the window. He stressed that he was not trying to downplay what happened and that Ryanair would await the findings of investigators.The US National Transportation Safety Board is leading the investigation. Boeing, which manufactured the aircraft, and GE, the engine manufacturer, are also involved.A preliminary investigation found that a fan blade from the aircraft’s right engine broke during the climb shortly after takeoff. Debris from the engine struck the aircraft and shattered the passenger window.The dispute over exactly what happened inside the cabin is therefore likely to depend on the findings of the NTSB investigation.O’Leary also said Karović would be entitled to “some compensation”, but disputed claims that the incident could justify a multimillion-euro payout.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
